# Pāsarāsi Sutta (MN 26 (PTS MN i 160))

**ID:** MN 26 (PTS MN i 160)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Pāsarāsi Sutta
**PTS:** MN i 160
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul2.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Pāsarāsi Sutta* (MN 26; PTS MN i 160) is preserved in the Burmese and Siamese traditions under the title *Pāsarāsi Sutta* ("Discourse on the Heap of Snares"), whereas Sinhalese manuscripts designate it as the *Ariyapariyesana Sutta* ("The Noble Search"); the commentary *Papañcasūdanī* records both titles [Anālayo 2014; Wynne 2007]. It represents one of the earliest and most foundational autobiographical accounts of the Buddha's spiritual quest found in the Pāli Canon [Hirakawa 1990; Radich 2007]. Structurally, it exhibits an intricate symmetry between the inner autobiographical narrative and the framing teaching setting [Galasek 2016].

Unlike later biographical traditions, it makes no explicit reference to the *bodhipakkhiyā dhammā* in this context, nor does its Chinese parallel apply the title *bodhisattva* to the pre-awakened Gautama [Anālayo 2014; Anālayo 2017].

Curated parallels and automated analyses demonstrate extensive cross-canonical reuse [DharmaNexus]. Curated parallels include Majjhima Nikāya discourses (MN 36, MN 85, MN 100), the Vinaya *Mahākhandhaka* (Kd 1), Sanskrit fragments of the *Catuṣpariṣatsūtra*, and versions in the *Madhyama Āgama* (MĀ 204), *Ekottarika Āgama* (EĀ 19.1, EĀ 24.5), *Lalitavistara*, and the *Saṅghabhedavastu* [Anālayo 2014]. DharmaNexus strongly aligns the text internally with MN 85 (over 65,000 shared characters), MN 36, MN 100, and Kd 1, and cross-linguistically with the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu*, the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (T 26), the Tibetan *Abhiniṣkramaṇa-sūtra*, and the *Mahāvastu* [DharmaNexus].
